sentences.text: Mapusaurus resembled Giganotosaurus but possessed a deeper skull, a rougher maxilla and lacrimal bone, and differently proportioned neck vertebrae.
This predator had very small arms proportionally similar to those of tyrannosaurids and abelisaurids.
The outer surface of the maxilla featured a rough texture, a trait shared with other carcharodontosaurids.
Unlike Giganotosaurus, where this texture stopped shortly behind the nasal opening, the rough surface on the Mapusaurus maxilla extended for most of the bone's length.
The first fossils were discovered in 1997 at Cañadón del Gato, located 20 km south of Plaza Huincul in Neuquén Province, Argentina.
Subsequent finds revealed a bonebed containing between seven and nine specimens within the Huincul Formation.
The genus was scientifically described in 2006 by Rodolfo Coria and Philip J. Currie.
The only described species is Mapusaurus roseae, named for the rose-colored rocks of its discovery site and its sponsor, Rose Letwin.
The largest known specimen, represented by a femur, was originally estimated to be 10.2 meters long and weigh 3 tons.
Later studies revised the maximum size estimates to between 10.2 and 12.6 meters in length and 6 to 8 tons in mass.
In 2016, Coria suggested that Mapusaurus may have hunted in groups to take down large prey like Argentinosaurus, similar to Giganotosaurus.
A cervical vertebra from the bonebed showed signs of an infection possibly similar to tuberculosis.
Mapusaurus is classified in the family Carcharodontosauridae, subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae, and tribe Giganotosaurini.
The tribe Giganotosaurini includes Mapusaurus, Meraxes, Giganotosaurus, and Tyrannotitan, but excludes the African genus Carcharodontosaurus.
Mapusaurus lived in Argentina during the Albian age of the Early Cretaceous.
The deposits of the Huincul Formation were laid down during the Lower Cretaceous.
Previously, the Cretaceous world was thought to be biogeographically separated with tyrannosaurids in the north, abelisaurids in South America, and carcharodontosaurids in Africa.
The subfamily Carcharodontosaurinae was likely restricted to Gondwana, where they were probably apex predators.
Some researchers have suggested that Taurovenator is a synonym of Mapusaurus because they found no unique distinguishing traits in Taurovenator.
Other researchers argue that Taurovenator and Mapusaurus are distinct genera because they come from different stratigraphic units of the Huincul Formation.
The different geological layers where the fossils were found support the argument that Taurovenator is a valid genus distinct from Mapusaurus.
It is debated whether Mapusaurus hunted in organized groups or simply attacked in bands, as the specific hunting mechanism remains unknown.
